turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I guess, well... it’s kind of a specific thing that finally pushed me to actually make the appointment and come in today. I mean, I’m a software developer, so my days are pretty much back-to-back screen time, especially on Mondays when we have our sprint planning meetings. Those can go on for an hour or two, mapping out all the coding tickets for the next two weeks, which is super important to get right, obviously. But I just... I keep getting up during them. 

And it’s not just work, it’s personal stuff too. Like, my husband and I are dealing with some house stuff right now and having these really dense mortgage calls where the loan officer is going over rates and escrow and all that, and even when I know I really, really should just stay put and pay attention, I just can't seem to stay in my chair. I’ll suddenly feel like I absolutely need to go get a glass of water right that exact second, or I’ll decide I need to check on something in the other room, like if I left a coffee mug on the counter or something completely trivial like that. 

And I just get up and walk away. My husband gets so frustrated with me, and I know my team is noticing on our video calls because my camera just keeps showing an empty chair. I tell myself before the call starts to just sit there, just stay in the seat, but it’s like I don't even realize I'm doing it until I'm already halfway to the kitchen. So, yeah, I just really need to figure out why I can't just sit through a normal meeting like everyone else.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly describes repeatedly leaving her seat during important work meetings and personal calls when she is expected to remain seated.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to school or earlier jobs, were you always able to sit through classes or meetings without feeling this urge to get up, or has this been a lifelong pattern for you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow, yeah. It’s definitely not a new thing. I mean, when I really think about it, it goes all the way back to when I was just a little kid. Like, elementary school. I vividly remember... well, I had this one teacher in third grade, and she actually had to physically move my desk right up next to hers at the front of the room. And even with me sitting right there under her nose, she was constantly having to remind me to just stay in my seat. 

Because I was always, always popping up. I’d finish a worksheet and immediately stand up to go sharpen my pencil, or I’d just wander over to the reading corner, or I'd get up to look at what the kid next to me was doing. And it wasn’t because I didn't get the material, you know? I actually understood the work perfectly fine, but I would just completely rush through everything. I’d fly through a math sheet or a spelling test just so I could be done with it, even though I knew how to do it right, and then I'd just be up and out of my chair again the second my pencil went down. 

And the talking, too—I was terrible about that. The teacher would ask a question to the class, and before she could even finish calling on someone, or before I even had my hand halfway up, I would just blurt out the answer. I just couldn't hold it in or wait my turn. So, yeah, it’s like my brain just couldn't handle the waiting part of school. I guess I've always been like this, just constantly in motion or jumping ahead of everyone else, and it just... it really hasn't changed, has it? Even now with my work meetings, it's that exact same feeling of just needing to move or do something else right that exact second.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes constantly popping up out of their chair and wandering around the classroom when they were expected to stay seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient mentions experiencing an intense, persistent feeling of needing to move during work meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient states they have always been 'constantly in motion'.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient admits they were 'terrible' about talking in class.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they would 'blurt out the answer' before the teacher finished calling on someone.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient notes they 'just couldn't hold it in or wait my turn' in class.

turns.doctor_question: When you're working on your coding projects or trying to focus on detailed tasks, do you find it hard to concentrate or keep your attention on one thing, or do you find yourself making careless mistakes even when you understand what you're supposed to be doing?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it’s funny you ask that, because I’ve been thinking a lot about how I actually do my work lately. Like, okay, take reviewing a pull request, for example. That’s a huge part of my job. I’ll sit down, open up the code, and I really, truly have the best intentions. I tell myself, "Okay, we’re going to sit here, we’re going to look at this logic, we’re going to make sure there are no bugs." And for the first, I don't know, two or three minutes, I’m right there. I’m in it. But then... it’s like my brain just slips on a banana peel or something. 

I’ll realize that I’ve been staring at the exact same block of code, or the exact same paragraph if it's those dense mortgage documents my husband and I are dealing with, for who knows how long. And I’m not even reading it anymore. My eyes are on the screen, but my mind is completely gone. I’ll be thinking about, like, five completely unrelated things at once. I’ll be wondering if I remembered to run the dishwasher, and then that makes me think about how we need more detergent, which makes me think about going to the store, and then I'm suddenly planning out my entire weekend errand route in my head while I’m supposed to be checking for syntax errors. 

And then I have to physically shake my head and force myself to scroll back up and start all over again, because I have absolutely no idea what I just read. It’s so frustrating because it’s not that the work is too hard, or that I don’t understand the mortgage terms—I mean, I do, mostly—it’s just that I literally cannot keep my brain tethered to the page. It just floats away the second it gets even a little bit bored. And it happens all the time, every single day, no matter how much I try to just buckle down and focus.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain focus on tasks like reviewing code or reading documents for more than a few minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly mentions becoming distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as chores and errands, while trying to work.

turns.doctor_question: When you're working on coding projects that you find really interesting or engaging—something that genuinely captures your attention—do you still have that same problem with your mind wandering and losing focus, or does it tend to be mainly when you're doing something more boring or repetitive?
turns.patient_response:
You know, that's a really interesting question, and I've actually thought about that a lot, especially when I'm trying to figure out why I'm like this. Because, you'd think, right? You'd think if it was just a problem with my brain being broken, it would happen all the time, no matter what. But honestly... I'm not really sure. I mean, I don't really know if it's different when it's something I'm super interested in versus something boring. 

Like, if I'm building out a new feature from scratch, which is usually the fun part of my job—the creative part where I'm really getting in the weeds of the architecture—I still feel like I'm bouncing all over the place. But then again, maybe I'm not? Maybe I am actually hyper-focused and I just don't realize it because I'm so deep in the code? Or maybe I'm still getting up to get water and checking my phone and thinking about the dishwasher, but I just don't notice it as much because I'm actually enjoying the work? 

It's so hard to say, because when I'm in the middle of it, I'm not really analyzing my own brain, you know? I'm just trying to get the code to compile. And with the boring stuff, like the mortgage documents or the pull requests, it's just so glaringly obvious that I can't focus, because I'm actively fighting it. I'm sitting there going, "Read the words, read the words," and my brain is just screaming, "No, let's think about grocery shopping!" 

So, yeah, I guess I really haven't noticed if there's a clear difference. It feels like a struggle pretty much across the board, but maybe it just manifests differently depending on how much I actually want to be doing the thing? I don't know, it's a really good question, but I just don't have a clear answer for you. It all just feels like a blur of me trying to keep myself on track, no matter what the track actually is.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a constant struggle to keep themselves on track and maintain focus, regardless of whether the task is interesting or boring.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly mentions being distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as thinking about the dishwasher or grocery shopping, while trying to work.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of work and meetings, do you find it hard to keep track of things—like remembering appointments, keeping your house organized, or planning out your day—or do those kinds of organizational and planning tasks come pretty naturally to you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow. Naturally? No. Definitely, definitely not naturally. It is... well, it’s honestly a complete disaster if I’m being completely transparent with you. It’s funny you mention keeping track of things because my husband and I were just talking about this, especially with all the house stuff we’re trying to manage right now. You would think, being a software developer, I’d have this perfectly optimized, streamlined system for my life, right? Like some beautiful, perfectly tagged digital board where everything flows perfectly. But no, it is absolute chaos. 

If you were to look at how I manage my life right now, it’s just... it’s everywhere. My work tickets for my current sprint are in one place, but then my home repair notes—because we're trying to fix up a few things around the house—are completely separate, and then our budget reminders are somewhere else entirely. And none of it is centralized! It’s all just completely scattered between Slack messages I’ve saved for later and then immediately forgotten about, a million neon sticky notes physically framing my computer monitor, emails I’ve sent to myself at two in the morning so I wouldn't forget something, and like, twelve different random, untitled lists in the Notes app on my phone. 

And the worst part—the part that drives me and my husband absolutely crazy—is that because everything is so fragmented like that, I end up spending way, way more time just trying to figure out what I was supposed to do than actually doing the things! Like, I’ll sit down on a Saturday morning, and I know I have things to get done, but I have to spend an hour just cross-referencing my phone, my email, and my desk just to piece together my actual to-do list. I'll find a sticky note that just says "call about the thing," and I have to go digging through my Slack to figure out if that was a work thing or an email to figure out if it was a budget thing. By the time I finally figure out what my tasks actually are, I'm already mentally exhausted. So no, organizing and planning definitely do not come naturally. It's like I have to go on a scavenger hunt every single day just to figure out my own life, and it is so incredibly draining.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states that organizing and planning do not come naturally, describing her task management as 'absolute chaos' with notes scattered across multiple platforms.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions saving messages for later and immediately forgetting about them, and needing to send herself emails in the middle of the night so she won't forget things.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to your childhood and school years, besides the difficulty sitting still and blurting things out, did you also struggle with things like losing your belongings, forgetting instructions, or having trouble organizing tasks—or was the main issue really just the physical restlessness and impulsivity?
turns.patient_response:
You know, looking back... it's interesting, because I don't really remember the losing things or the forgetting instructions being the big red flags back then. I mean, maybe my mom just managed all my stuff for me so I didn't notice, but the main issue—the thing that was always, always brought up at parent-teacher conferences—was absolutely the physical stuff. The restlessness. It was just so prominent. 

Like, I have these incredibly vivid memories from elementary school, especially around third or fourth grade, where my teachers were just constantly having to intervene. They were always moving my desk. They would physically separate me from the rest of the class, or put my desk right up against theirs at the front of the room, just so they could constantly remind me to stay seated. Because I just couldn't! I was always popping up out of my chair. It was like I had springs in my legs or something. If I had a thought, I was standing up. 

And the talking... oh my gosh, I was always talking before I was called on. The teacher would ask a question to the class, and I wouldn't even think to raise my hand, I would just blurt out the answer the second it popped into my head. It drove them crazy. And it wasn't because I was struggling academically or didn't get it. I actually understood the work perfectly fine! But I would just rush through things at lightning speed. They'd hand out a worksheet and I would just blast through it, scribbling down whatever, just so I could be done and do something else or try to talk to the person next to me. Even when I knew exactly what I was supposed to be doing and understood the concepts, I just rushed it. 

So, yeah, it wasn't really the organizing tasks or losing my belongings that I remember struggling with as a kid, it was just this constant, overwhelming urge to move and talk and rush through every single thing. I just could not keep myself contained in that little plastic chair.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they were 'always popping up out of my chair' and teachers had to constantly remind them to stay seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms that physical restlessness was a prominent issue during childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes having a 'constant, overwhelming urge to move' and feeling like they had 'springs in my legs'.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient admits they would 'blurt out the answer the second it popped into my head' before being called on.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient denies that forgetting instructions was a significant issue for them as a child.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they do not remember struggling with organizing tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient denies that losing belongings was a problem they struggled with during childhood.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned that in childhood you were constantly moving around and blurting things out. When you think about yourself as a teenager or young adult—say, in high school or college—did those physical restlessness and impulsivity issues continue to be just as much of a problem, or did they get better as you got older?
turns.patient_response:
That’s... yeah, that’s a really good distinction to make. Because if you were to just look at me in high school, or especially later on in college—like when I was getting my computer science degree and had to sit through these massive, two-hour lectures on data structures or whatever—you would probably think, "Oh, she grew out of it. She's fine now." Because I wasn't literally popping out of my seat anymore, right? I wasn't running around the room or shouting out answers the way I did in fourth grade. Society kind of beats that out of you by the time you're a teenager. 

But did it actually get better? Honestly... no. It didn't go away at all. It just went inward, I guess? Like, I learned how to fake it. I learned how to sit there and look like a normal, attentive student. But the feeling itself never left. 

Even then, and honestly even now, I can be sitting there, looking perfectly calm on the outside—maybe I'm looking at the professor, or staring at my laptop screen in a meeting—but inside, I feel this intense, building pressure. It’s like this physical tightness in my chest and my arms. I’ll be sitting there and I just feel this overwhelming urge that I absolutely *need* to move, or I need to switch tasks, or I need to just... do something, anything, with my hands. 

I remember in college, I would grip my pen so hard my knuckles would turn white just to keep myself from tapping it on the desk and annoying everyone around me. Or I'd be destroying the edges of my notebook paper, just shredding it into tiny little pieces under the desk where no one could see. Because if I forced myself to just sit completely still and do nothing but listen, it literally felt like I was going to crawl right out of my skin. It’s this horrible, buzzing discomfort. 

So people would look at me and think I was doing totally fine, just a quiet young woman taking notes, but they had absolutely no idea how much mental energy it was taking just to keep my body glued to that chair. It's exhausting, really. You spend all this energy just trying to look still, and fighting that pressure, and then you realize you haven't actually heard a single word the professor said for the last twenty minutes because you were too busy trying not to shake your leg or bounce your foot. So, yeah, the running around the classroom definitely stopped, but that restlessness didn't get better... it just got trapped inside me.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes losing focus and not hearing a single word of a lecture for twenty minutes because she is so focused on trying to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes fidgeting behaviors such as shredding notebook paper, shaking her leg, and bouncing her foot.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes an intense internal restlessness, feeling a building pressure and an overwhelming urge to move that makes her feel like she will crawl out of her skin.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states she no longer pops out of her seat or runs around the room as she did in childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly notes that she stopped shouting out answers the way she did when she was younger.

turns.doctor_question: When you're doing something you really enjoy—like coding a feature you're excited about, or even just relaxing at home doing something fun—do you still feel that same internal buzzing and pressure to move, or does that restless feeling mainly show up when you're in situations where you're supposed to be sitting still?
turns.patient_response:
You know, that’s a really interesting question, because you would think—logically, right?—that if I’m doing something I actually want to do, that feeling would just magically disappear. But it really doesn't. 

Like, I can be working on a feature I am super excited about. Just last week, I was building this new API integration for our platform that I had literally been begging my manager to let me take the lead on for months. I was so pumped to finally dig into it. And I’m sitting there at my desk, and if you walked by, on the outside, I probably looked completely Zen. Totally focused, just a developer typing away calmly at her keyboard. But even then... even when I’m sitting calmly on the outside like that, I still feel this intense pressure inside. It’s like I absolutely need to move, or I need to switch tasks for just a second, or I need to do something else with my hands before I literally crawl out of my skin. 

And it is the exact same thing when I’m just trying to relax at home! My husband and I will sit down on a Friday night to watch a movie—and I mean a movie I *really* want to watch, something we’ve been planning to see all week. I’ll be sitting there on the couch, looking perfectly still, but inside? My chest is just humming. I’m sitting there thinking, "I need to get up, I need to check my phone, I need to go grab a glass of water, maybe I should fold the laundry while we watch this." I literally cannot just sit there and consume the movie without my hands doing something. I’ll start picking at the seams of the throw pillows, or I'll bring my laptop over to the couch and tell my husband I'm just going to "lightly browse" while we watch. 

Which, of course, drives him absolutely nuts because he's like, "Can't you just relax for two hours?" And I try to explain it to him, I really do, but it's hard for people to get if they don't experience it. Because they look at me and see a forty-year-old woman sitting quietly on a sofa, but they don't feel that engine running inside. It really doesn't matter if I'm in a horribly boring status meeting or doing my absolute favorite hobby in the world. That feeling of needing to shift gears, or move my hands, or just... *do* something... it's always there simmering under the surface. I really, really wish it would just turn off when I'm having fun, but yeah, no, it's pretty much a constant companion.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes needing to do something with her hands and picking at the seams of throw pillows while trying to watch a movie.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly confirms feeling an intense internal pressure to move and feeling like she will 'crawl out of her skin' even when sitting calmly.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes feeling an 'engine running inside' and a constant need to be doing something, which aligns with acting as if driven by a motor.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient denies a loss of interest by describing activities she is 'super excited about' and referring to her 'absolute favorite hobby in the world.'
